PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process.
Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot.
State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot.

PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process.
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot.
Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program's annual costs by 10 percent.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit.
If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor's summary to be included in the VIG.
If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.

Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes.
Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting "yes" would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they're on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting "yes" could also mean that Proposition 40 (the "billionaire tax"), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop.
41.
Voting "no" would mean that the state auditor's role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.

# Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax
As the debate about taxing billionaires to fund healthcare escalates, California voters also will face decisions about whether to approve two propositions that could cancel out the proposed wealth tax.
Those measures include Proposition 41, also known as the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act.
Supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes.
It also would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit.
Since this conflicts with the proposed wealth tax, opponents say it’s a “billionaire-funded smoke screen” that would block the billionaire tax.
...
### What will the measure do?
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot.
The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas.
Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution.
It began as Initiative #25-0041A, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office.
Prop.
41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures.
The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%.
If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution.
It began as Initiative #25-0041A, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office.
Prop.
41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures.
The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%.
If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.

41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone.” -Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce
PROP. 41: A BETTER DEAL FOR TAXPAYERS
Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes-it protects taxpayers’ interests:
• Reduces the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; • Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit-including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop. 41 ensures taxpayers get better results-not just a bigger tax bill.
“Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Californians already pay the highest state income and sales taxes in the country-we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results. Prop. 41 delivers.” -Steve Westly, former Controller of California.
Please join good government groups, small business owners, accountants, taxpayers and public transparency advocates in voting Yes on 41.
For more information, visit: www.ResultsCA.org

ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone.” -Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce
PROP. 41: A BETTER DEAL FOR TAXPAYERS
Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes-it protects taxpayers’ interests:
• Reduces the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; • Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit-including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop. 41 ensures taxpayers get better results-not just a bigger tax bill.
“Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Californians already pay the highest state income and sales taxes in the country-we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results. Prop. 41 delivers.” -Steve Westly, former Controller of California.
Please join good government groups, small business owners, accountants, taxpayers and public transparency advocates in voting Yes on 41.
For more information, visit: www.ResultsCA.org
Denise LeDuc Froemming , CPA, President
California Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs)
Tom Hayes , Fmr. California State Auditor

California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 41
VOTE NO ON PROP. 41. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 41 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing new taxes. It’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 41 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 41 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 41 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 41 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 41.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West

PROPOSITION 41
When state government programs don’t deliver, it hurts the people who rely on those services and the taxpayers who fund them.
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by new taxes-to help make programs more effective and efficient.
Ask yourself: why would a single, solitary Sacramento special interest oppose transparency and accountability?
YES ON 41: TAXPAYERS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS
Some facts:
• Our state budget is a record high $352 billion this year. • State spending is up 79% since 2019. • We’ve spent billions on programs like homelessness-with too little to show for it.
With some of the highest taxes in the nation and a rising cost of living, we can’t afford to fund failure. Every dollar wasted is one that could go to help someone.
Prop. 41 requires transparency and trackable progress of programs, to help improve education, health care and other public services Californians rely on.
PROP. 41: PUBLIC AUDITS TO IMPROVE ACCOUNTABILITY
“Independent performance audits give voters objective, credible information about public resources, strengthening accountability and public trust.” Denise LeDuc Froemming, President, California Society of Certified Public Accountants
Under Prop. 41, the independent State Auditor publicly reviews the programs that new taxes would fund, exposes any waste or mismanagement, and recommends program improvements. The audit findings are published in the Voter Information Guide before you vote-with ongoing audits if a tax is approved.
VOTERS DESERVE MORE TRANSPARENCY-even if special interests don’t like it.
Vote Yes on Prop. 41. More transparency, more accountability, better results for our tax dollars.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.

Now I have the analysis and arguments. Key facts:

Proposition 41 (Nov 3, 2026 California General Election):
1. Requires one-time pre-ballot audits by the State Auditor of programs funded by proposed new special taxes via voter initiative (triggered at 25% of signature threshold).
2. Requires ongoing audits every 4 years of programs funded by special taxes created/increased after Jan 1, 2026 (by Legislature or voters).
3. Prohibits new state taxes (after Jan 1, 2026) from being excluded from the state appropriations limit (Gann Limit) — this is the key provision. It would "nullify" state taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempt revenues from the Gann Limit.

The context: Proposition 40 is the "California Billionaire Tax" — a one-time wealth tax on billionaires (~200 of them) to fund healthcare (backed by SEIU-UHW). The billionaire tax presumably exempts its revenues from the Gann Limit. Prop 41 was funded largely by Sergey Brin (Google co-founder) who spent $57M+ to fund measures to counteract the billionaire tax. If Prop 41 gets more yes votes than Prop 40 (and both pass), Prop 41 could block/conflict with Prop 40 — courts would determine, or the measure with more votes prevails on conflicting provisions.

- Who funded Prop 41 (campaign finance)
- News coverage: LA Times, CalMatters, etc.
- The relationship between Prop 40 and Prop 41
- Editorial board positions
- Details on how Prop 41 would block Prop 40

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> As the debate about taxing billionaires to fund healthcare escalates, California voters also will face decisions about whether to approve two propositions that could cancel out the proposed wealth tax.
Those measures include Proposition 41, also known as the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act.
Supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes. It also would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Since this conflicts with the proposed wealth tax, opponents say it’s a “billionaire-funded smoke screen” that would block the billionaire tax.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas. Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit. That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.

Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The bulk of the contributions to support the proposition have come from Building a Better California, data from the California secretary of state’s website show. Top contributors to Building a Better California include Sergey Brin, Google’s co-founder; John Doerr, chairman of venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins; and Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google.
Advertisement
Proposition 41 “requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes,” a website for the proposition states.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41.
In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.
“This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce,” Jimenez wrote.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The proposition states its purpose is to make sure that “programs are delivering results, and that taxpayer dollars are not being lost to inefficiency, waste or abuse.” Opponents say the proposition is meant to nullify the proposed billionaire tax.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> As the debate about taxing billionaires to fund healthcare escalates, California voters also will face decisions about whether to approve two propositions that could cancel out the proposed wealth tax.
Those measures include Proposition 41, also known as the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act.
Supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes. It also would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Since this conflicts with the proposed wealth tax, opponents say it’s a “billionaire-funded smoke screen” that would block the billionaire tax.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas. Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit. That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.

Now I have a very clear picture. Let me summarize what I've learned:

**Proposition 41** (November 3, 2026 California General Election):
- Officially: "Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment."
- Also known as "Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act"

**Provisions:**
1. Requires State Auditor to review programs funded by new/increased special taxes proposed via voter initiatives (after 25% of signatures collected), with summary in the VIG. Audits must identify ways to cut program costs by 10%.
2. Ongoing audits every 4 years of programs funded by special taxes created/increased after Jan 1, 2026.
3. Prohibits/nullifies new state taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempt revenues from the Gann Limit (state appropriations/spending limit).

**Context/Intent:**
- Prop 40 is the "California Billionaire Tax" — a one-time 5% wealth tax on ~250 billionaires to fund healthcare (backed by SEIU-UHW), which explicitly exempts its revenues from the Gann Limit.
- Prop 41 (and Prop 42) are "poison pill" measures funded by billionaires (Sergey Brin $102M, Eric Schmidt, John Doerr, Patrick Collison, Vinod Khosla via "Building a Better California" — $300M+ total spending) designed to nullify Prop 40. Under California law, when two conflicting measures pass, the one with more yes votes prevails on conflicting provisions. Prop 41 explicitly states it would nullify Prop 40 if it gets more votes.
- Supporters: CalTax, CalCPAs, CalAsian Chamber, Steve Westly, Tom Hayes (former State Auditor)
- Opponents: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders

**Arguments:**
- Pro: transparency, accountability, audits of programs funded by new taxes; all taxes should comply with voter-approved Gann Limit spending rules.
- Con: It's a billionaire-funded deception to kill the billionaire tax; audit requirements are designed to stall/weaken programs; the audits at 25% signature collection could burden the initiative process; the Gann Limit provision is the real intent, and it could also impair future taxes for education/healthcare; audits cost money (low millions/year, some from General Fund for measures that don't qualify).

**Editorial positions:**
- SF Chronicle: No — "cynical poison pill"
- East Bay Times published a "Yes" campaign piece (that's the campaign's own writing, not necessarily an endorsement)
- LA Times news coverage describes it neutrally but notes it "could block billionaire tax"

Now, the question: Should I recommend yes or no? The user asks me to come to my own decision after research and answer with only "yes" or "no".

Let me think about the merits:

**On the merits of the audit provisions:** Audits of programs funded by new special taxes sound reasonable — transparency and accountability. But there are wrinkles:
- The pre-election audit at 25% signature threshold means the State Auditor must audit programs that don't even exist yet (programs *proposed* to be funded), before the measure even qualifies. Auditing a hypothetical program and requiring recommendations to cut its costs by 10% is an unusual design that seems aimed at creating negative fodder in the voter guide against tax initiatives. It would also cost the General Fund money for initiatives that never qualify.
- The ongoing audits every 4 years are paid from the tax revenue itself, diverting program funds.
- The State Auditor already has authority to audit government programs; the Legislature can request audits via JLAC (Joint Legislative Audit Committee). So the audit function largely exists.

**On the Gann Limit provision:** This is the consequential part. It would nullify any state tax enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempts revenues from the Gann Limit. This is retroactive and targeted at Prop 40. The Gann Limit, when exceeded, requires rebates to taxpayers or spending on certain purposes. Prop 40's design (exempting from Gann) is intended to let the state actually spend the revenue on healthcare rather than triggering rebates/spending-limit complications.

**The poison pill mechanics:** Prop 41 contains language that explicitly nullifies Prop 40 if both pass and 41 gets more votes. It's part of a $300M+ billionaire-funded campaign. The measure was designed and bankrolled by the people who would be taxed by Prop 40 — a clear self-interest motivation. The "audit" framing is widely characterized as a smoke screen by opponents, and even neutral coverage (LA Times, Sac Bee, SF Chronicle, Mother Jones, Forbes, Fortune, HuffPost, SFGate) characterizes these as poison pills designed to kill Prop 40.

**Weighing:**
- If one supports the billionaire tax (Prop 40) or at least wants voters' decision on Prop 40 to stand on its own merits, a yes on 41 undermines it via a deceptive side-channel.
- The audit provisions, while superficially appealing, are of dubious design: auditing programs before they exist, mandating a 10% cost-cut finding (prescriptive and biased toward cuts), diverting program funds to audits, and adding costs. They also duplicate existing State Auditor/JLAC functions.
- The constitutional amendment locks these provisions in, making them hard to change.
- The retroactivity/targeting (Jan 1, 2026 effective date) is transparently aimed at one measure, which is generally bad governance — using the constitution to settle a discrete political fight.
- The Gann Limit provision would apply to all future taxes, constraining the state's fiscal flexibility (e.g., future taxes for education, wildfire response, healthcare) and potentially forcing rebates rather than allowing dedicated spending approved by voters. When voters approve a special tax for a purpose, they'd expect the money to be spent on that purpose; forcing it under the Gann Limit could mean the money can't actually be spent as voters intended.

Counterpoints (steel-manning yes):
- Transparency/accountability for programs funded by new taxes is genuinely valuable; California has documented waste issues (homelessness spending audits found poor tracking).
- Gann Limit compliance ensures taxpayer rebates when the state collects more than the spending limit — a taxpayer protection voters approved in 1979.
- Supported by CPAs, taxpayer association, former State Auditor.

But on balance: The measure is a targeted poison pill with deceptive framing, constitutional rigidity, dubious audit design (pre-qualification audits of hypothetical programs, mandatory 10% cut findings), funding from self-interested billionaires specifically to thwart another measure on the same ballot, and it constrains future voter-approved taxes' ability to be spent as intended. The SF Chronicle editorial board called it a "cynical poison pill." Most good-government framing is undermined by the fact that existing mechanisms (State Auditor, JLAC) can already audit programs without a constitutional amendment.

Also consider: if a voter likes the billionaire tax, voting yes on 41 could nullify their own yes vote on 40. If a voter dislikes the billionaire tax, they can simply vote no on 40 — they don't need 41. Prop 41's marginal effect beyond the ballot box on 40 is to override the will of the majority on Prop 40 via vote-count gamesmanship.

Hmm, but wait — should I also consider the perspective of someone who opposes the billionaire tax on the merits? For them, Prop 41 is a backstop. But even so, good governance suggests defeating measures directly rather than through confusing poison pills. And the audit regime's design flaws remain regardless.

**Editorial positions:**
- SF Chronicle: No — "cynical poison pill"
- East Bay Times published a "Yes" campaign piece (that's the campaign's own writing, not necessarily an endorsement)
- LA Times news coverage describes it neutrally but notes it "could block billionaire tax"

Let me think about the merits:

**On the merits of the audit provisions:** Audits of programs funded by new special taxes sound reasonable — transparency and accountability. But there are wrinkles:
- The pre-election audit at 25% signature threshold means the State Auditor must audit programs that don't even exist yet (programs *proposed* to be funded), before the measure even qualifies. Auditing a hypothetical program and requiring recommendations to cut its costs by 10% is an unusual design that seems aimed at creating negative fodder in the voter guide against tax initiatives. It would also cost the General Fund money for initiatives that never qualify.
- The ongoing audits every 4 years are paid from the tax revenue itself, diverting program funds.
- The State Auditor already has authority to audit government programs; the Legislature can request audits via JLAC (Joint Legislative Audit Committee). So the audit function largely exists.

This is retroactive and targeted at Prop 40. The Gann Limit, when exceeded, requires rebates to taxpayers or spending on certain purposes. Prop 40's design (exempting from Gann) is intended to let the state actually spend the revenue on healthcare rather than triggering rebates/spending-limit complications.

**The poison pill mechanics:** Prop 41 contains language that explicitly nullifies Prop 40 if both pass and 41 gets more votes. It's part of a $300M+ billionaire-funded campaign. The measure was designed and bankrolled by the people who would be taxed by Prop 40 — a clear self-interest motivation. The "audit" framing is widely characterized as a smoke screen by opponents, and even neutral coverage (LA Times, Sac Bee, SF Chronicle, Mother Jones, Forbes, Fortune, HuffPost, SFGate) characterizes these as poison pills designed to kill Prop 40.

**Weighing:**
- If one supports the billionaire tax (Prop 40) or at least wants voters' decision on Prop 40 to stand on its own merits, a yes on 41 undermines it via a deceptive side-channel.
- The audit provisions, while superficially appealing, are of dubious design: auditing programs before they exist, mandating a 10% cost-cut finding (prescriptive and biased toward cuts), diverting program funds to audits, and adding costs. They also duplicate existing State Auditor/JLAC functions.
- The constitutional amendment locks these provisions in, making them hard to change.
- The retroactivity/targeting (Jan 1, 2026 effective date) is transparently aimed at one measure, which is generally bad governance — using the constitution to settle a discrete political fight.
- The Gann Limit provision would apply to all future taxes, constraining the state's fiscal flexibility (e.g., future taxes for education, wildfire response, healthcare) and potentially forcing rebates rather than allowing dedicated spending approved by voters. When voters approve a special tax for a purpose, they'd expect the money to be spent on that purpose; forcing it under the Gann Limit could mean the money can't actually be spent as voters intended.

Counterpoints (steel-manning yes):
- Transparency/accountability for programs funded by new taxes is genuinely valuable; California has documented waste issues (homelessness spending audits found poor tracking).

The SF Chronicle editorial board called it a "cynical poison pill." Most good-government framing is undermined by the fact that existing mechanisms (State Auditor, JLAC) can already audit programs without a constitutional amendment.

Also consider: if a voter likes the billionaire tax, voting yes on 41 could nullify their own yes vote on 40. If a voter dislikes the billionaire tax, they can simply vote no on 40 — they don't need 41. Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.
